_comment: Levels a person decided, and the reason for each.
Two kinds of row. One carries a `level` and moves the word; the other
carries `keep: true` and says the model's level is right and the check that
flagged it was reading the wrong evidence. Both are decisions somebody made
and can be argued with, which is the point — a weight nudged until one word
moves is a decision nobody can find later.
`vocabulary:level:qa` skips its contamination checks for any word listed
here, because a listed word has already been looked at. It does not skip the
anchor check: an anchor is a stronger statement than an override and if the
two disagree the disagreement should be visible.

September 2026: eighteen rows added at once, which is unusual and is why they are described together. All eighteen are words with editorial usefulness 1 — the highest — and a frequency rank inside the commonest 1,200, sitting at levels 7 to 14. They share one cause: `_concreteness` in scripts/content/level.py returns a fixed weight for any tag whose template is in ABSTRACT_TEMPLATES and never looks at the parts, so every `cmp:` antonym pair and every `seq:` before-and-after pair is scored unpicturable. 길다, 짧다, 멀다, 가깝다, 열다 and 닫다 are among the most picturable words in the language.

They are moved here rather than by changing the weight, because changing it re-levels the whole corpus and would have to be re-anchored and re-read; that is the right fix and it is a piece of work, not a nudge. The model defect is recorded as an open issue so this is a decision on the record and not a workaround nobody can find.

그들.why: Written Korean. Spoken Korean says 그 사람들 or drops the subject entirely, and a learner who says 그들이 in conversation sounds like a subtitle. The frequency corpora are subtitles, which is exactly why they rank it high.

저.why: Flagged literary because Wiktionary's first pronoun sense for this spelling is the distal demonstrative, not the humble first person this app teaches. The taught sense is the most ordinary word in polite Korean and level 1 is right.

잇다.why: The frequency matcher gives it rank 1, which is wrong: it folds every token ending in a verb suffix that begins 이- or 잇- onto this stem. 잇다 is an ordinary but not common verb and the other three components put it here.

잘다.why: Rank 296 for the same reason — 잘 is a very frequent adverb and tokens like 잘게 and 잘지 fold onto this stem. 잘다 itself is uncommon and mostly written.

크다.why: The model puts it at 10 on polysemy: 크다 is big, and grows, and is a lot. A beginner meets the first sense in week one and the others years later, and the card teaches the first.

그녀.why: Written Korean, like 그들. Common in subtitles because subtitles are written; a beginner should learn 그 사람 first and will not be understood using 그녀 in speech.

월.why: The month word every date carries: a learner reads 3월 in their first weeks. The frequency fold only ever sees it fused into month names (삼월, 유월), so the model files it as rare when it is bound-but-everywhere. Same class as 감사합니다 (I-73).

아이디어.why: An English loanword whose meaning costs nothing once sounded out; the model's semantic-abstraction term prices it like an abstract Sino noun. A learner who can read Hangul owns this word immediately.

모르다.why: Frequency rank 46 — the 46th commonest word in the corpus — and the partner of 알다, which is level 1. A beginner says 몰라요 on their first day.

열다.why: Same cause as the `cmp:` words: its tag is a `seq:` before-and-after pair, which `_concreteness` weights 0.75 flat. A door opening is about as picturable as Korean gets, and this is first-month vocabulary.

닫다.why: Same cause as the `cmp:` words: its tag is a `seq:` before-and-after pair, which `_concreteness` weights 0.75 flat. A door opening is about as picturable as Korean gets, and this is first-month vocabulary.

놀다.why: Tagged `solo:game`, and *game* is not in the concrete-parts list, so it falls to the 0.35 default. This file's own comment already records 놀다 as the example of that mis-scoring and moved it from 19 to 11; 11 is still six levels above 친구 and 같이.

길다.why: The model scores this abstract because its semantic tag is a `cmp:` antonym pair, and `_concreteness` returns a template's fixed weight without ever consulting the parts — so a word is called unpicturable for having an opposite. Having an opposite says nothing about whether you can see it: this is first-semester vocabulary in every Korean course and a learner meets it in the first month.

맛있다.why: The build's own docstring names this word as the failure the difficulty split was written to fix — it was at level 10 under the single-number model and it is at level 10 again. 밥, 음식 and 먹다 are all level 3, and 맛있어요 is what a learner says about them.

가르치다.why: Rank 664, usefulness 1, and the partner of 배우다. 선생님 is level 4; the verb belongs beside it.

어렵다.why: Rank 514. The pair 쉽다/어렵다 is taught in the first month and 쉽다 is at level 6; a five-level gap between two halves of one pair is a gap a learner notices.

착하다.why: Rank 1076, usefulness 1. Not first-month, but 12 is where the model puts words a learner meets in their second year.
